beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Adwait Changan, and this video is about a pull request that went red without me touching it. Today we are going to learn how to tell whose failure you are actually looking at. My branch had drifted months behind, and when I caught it up, eleven files conflicted and nineteen checks failed. Almost none of it was mine.

show.event: composer on cream; the fellow names himself and the subject

props.command: My pull request is red. How much of this is actually mine?
output: Eleven conflicts after catching up with the main branch.
Nineteen failing checks, none of them in files I wrote.
The useful skill is not fixing it. It is proving whose it is.

beats.act: ACT 1 — RED IS NOT A DIAGNOSIS
beats.narration_text: A failing pull request tells you something is wrong and nothing about where. There are only three possibilities and they need completely different responses. The failure is yours. It belongs to someone else and you inherited it. Or it was already broken before you arrived.

show.event: 'It was already broken' lands in terracotta

layers.title: It is yours
layers.sub: your commits introduced it; fix it

layers.title: You inherited it
layers.sub: it arrived with someone else's work; do not silently revert them

layers.title: It was already broken
layers.sub: the base branch fails too; fixing it is a separate job

props.caption: Red tells you none of these. You have to prove which one.

beats.act: ACT 1 — RED IS NOT A DIAGNOSIS
beats.narration_text: So I counted before touching anything. Eleven conflicting files. Ten of them under a gateway directory added by another contributor, which my branch had picked up through an old rebase. One genuinely shared file. And the number of my own commits that touch that gateway directory is zero.

show.event: the zero lands last in terracotta

beats.narration_text: So the rule I used was simple. For every file I did not write, take the main branch version whole, then prove it. After resolving, the diff between my branch and main across that directory is empty. Not reviewed and probably fine. Empty.

show.event: 'Confirm it is empty' completes the grid

items: Identify every file you did not write
Take the base branch version whole
Diff your result against the base
props.caption: "Probably fine" is not the same as an empty diff.

beats.act: ACT 3 — THE CHECKS WERE ALREADY RED
beats.narration_text: What I did do was write all of it down in the merge commit. Which files were whose, why each was resolved the way it was, and that the remaining failure reproduces on the base branch. The next person to look at this should not have to repeat the investigation.

props.title: Write Down Whose It Was
props.body: Which files were whose, why each was resolved that way, and that the remaining failure reproduces on the base branch. Nobody should repeat the investigation.
props.sparkLine: In the commit, not your head.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. A red pull request tells you something is wrong and nothing about whose it is, and there are three answers that need completely different responses. Eleven files conflicted; ten belonged to another contributor and my own commits touched none of them, so I took the base branch version whole and proved the difference was empty rather than assuming it. The one genuinely shared file was an append-only log, so both sides were kept and the ordering verified. The nineteen failing checks reproduce on the base branch across five consecutive runs, so they were inherited, not caused. I left them alone and wrote down why.

show.event: the inherited-not-caused line holds in terracotta

props.artifactHeading: Prove whose failure it is before fixing it
artifactLines: Red means something is wrong. It says nothing about whose, and the three answers differ.
Ten of eleven conflicts were another contributor's. My commits touched none of those files.
Took the base version whole, then proved the diff was empty rather than assuming.
The shared append-only log kept both sides; ordering was verified, not trusted.
Nineteen failing checks reproduce on the base branch. Inherited, not caused. Left alone.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt. My branch is failing. Before suggesting any fix, tell me for each failure whether it reproduces on the base branch, which commits introduced the files involved, and whether any of them are mine. Then tell me which failures I should not touch. Run that the next time something goes red. The last question is the one that saves you from reverting a colleague by accident.

props.command: My branch is failing. Before suggesting any fix: for each failure, does it reproduce on the base branch, which commits introduced the files involved, and are any of them mine? Then tell me which failures I should not touch.
output: "Does it reproduce on the base branch" settles most of these in one command.
The failures you should not touch are the ones that save you from reverting a colleague.
